title: Molecular resolution fluorescence imaging: from Abbe to Ångström
content: Fluorescence microscopy has transformed molecular imaging in cells by combining molecular specificity with live-cell compatibility. Yet the classical diffraction limit has long obscured nanoscale imaging of the organization of protein complexes, nucleic acids, membranes, and intracellular assemblies within their native cellular context. This Review provides a chemistry-focused overview of super-resolution microscopy (SRM) strategies that enable spatial resolution down to the molecular level in cells, alongside emerging approaches that achieve Ångström-scale localization precision under selected experimental conditions. We start with a brief introduction into the historic development of fluorescence microscopy and its basic principles followed by methods that can be used to manipulate photophysics of fluorophores. Following the introduction of classical deterministic (SIM, STED, RESOLFT) and stochastic single-molecule localization microscopy (PALM, (d)STORM, DNA-PAINT) we summarize recent developments that achieved Ångström localization precision on isolated samples (RESI, MINFLUX). The summary of SRM techniques will be concluded with describing the potential of expansion microscopy (ExM) as a game changer towards multicolor three-dimensional (3D) molecular resolution fluorescence imaging. We further emphasize that progress in fluorophore engineering, photoswitching and photoactivation, labeling chemistry, buffer design, and analysis workflows remains central to maximizing resolution, photostability, and multiplexing capacity for all SRM methods. We highlight key applications in protein interactomics, chromatin organization, membrane biophysics, viral assembly, and single-molecule catalysis, together with persistent challenges in labeling fidelity, phototoxicity, temporal resolution, and 3D imaging. Finally, we discuss how combining expansion microscopy (ExM) and SRM can improve the separation of densely packed molecular features in cells, while distinguishing molecular-scale resolution from Ångström-scale localization precision and submolecular structural resolution.
